title: Capacity contract talking points (Dedicated)
body:
Purpose:
This note collects concise, procurement-facing talking points, likely legal/finance redlines, and commercial tactics for selling Redwood Dedicated capacity (reserved GPU pools). Focus is on predictable throughput, SLA / isolation guarantees, and procurement readiness. Use as an internal cheat-sheet for Sales Engineers, AEs, and Solutions teams during contract negotiations and procurement reviews.

Elevator pitch (one-liner):
Redwood Dedicated gives your team an SLA-backed, isolated GPU pool with predictable throughput and deterministic per-token economics — so production LLM features run at scale without unexpected latency or cost variability.

Top-level value props for procurement:
- Deterministic capacity: committed GPU allocation with defined throughput envelopes and burst policy; peak planning becomes a procurement problem, not an ops scramble.
- Isolation and data boundaries: tenant isolation, VPC peering options, single-tenant control plane for audit and compliance scopes.
- SLA-backed availability and latency targets: uptime and P99 token-latency objectives with financial credits for material breaches.
- Predictable unit economics: reserved pricing with clear overage/burst terms, smoothing consumption spikes and simplifying budgeting.
- Enterprise-grade ops: prioritized capacity, enhanced observability exports, and dedicated support windows for incident response.

Procurement talking points (concise bullets to present to Legal/Finance):
- Commitment model: 12/24/36 month reserved-sku contracts with quarterly usage true-ups.
- Billing: monthly invoice with line items for reserved capacity, metered overage (if enabled), and optional premium observability/retention add-ons.
- Credits and remedies: financial credits tied to SLA targets (availability and latency); escalation timeline and credit calculation formula included in SOW.
- Termination: early termination triggers and pro-rated refunds for hardware-backed commitments; standard negotiation levers are phase-out windows and transition assistance.
- Data controls: explicit clause for data residency, KMS integration, and audit log delivery cadence.

SLA & technical guarantees (candidate language for commercial terms):
- Availability: 99.95% monthly uptime for Dedicated cluster control plane and serving endpoints; definition of downtime excludes scheduled maintenance with ≥72h notice.
- Latency: P99 per-request inference latency objective ≤ X ms for baseline model profile (define per contract with model class and sequence length assumptions).
- Throughput: Guaranteed sustained token throughput (tokens/s) per reserved GPU pool; measured and reported hourly; sustained shortfalls >Y% over a 12-hour rolling window trigger remediation and credit.
- Isolation: single-tenant compute pools logically and physically isolated from other customers; dedicated NVLink/VPC attachments where applicable.
- Fallback policy: automated degradations to compatible model variants (quantized/low-memory profile) to uphold availability SLOs during partial capacity events — subject to customer opt-in.

Common procurement objections and rebuttals:
- "We don’t want to lock in a long commitment." -> Offer phased ramp commitments (lower initial reserve + staged increases) and defined exit/transition assistance.
- "How do you quantify throughput vs our workload?" -> Propose a short technical proof-of-work (POW): 2–4 week soak test using a customer workload profile with acceptance metrics for p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec. POW results feed the final throughput SLA.
- "What happens during spikes?" -> Explain burst pools (contractual burst credits) and automatic burst-to-hosted fallback with cost and latency expectations spelled out.
- "We need strict data controls." -> Detail KMS/HSM options, VPC-only control plane, and privileged access review processes (SOC2/ISO artifacts ready).

Negotiation play tracks (sales strategy):
- Velocity track (rapid close): 12-month reserve, standard SLA, higher $/token uplift for burst; minimal legal changes.
- Enterprise-risk-averse track: 24–36 month reserve, extended observability and SLAs, stronger termination/transition assistance, dedicated success manager.
- Flex/Ramp track: Lower committed baseline plus predictable ramp schedule + staged credits for early termination; POW required before final SLA sign-off.

Finance/COGS talking points for procurement teams:
- Unit economics: reserved capacity decouples cloud GPU spot volatility from your per-token cost — we guarantee a baseline unit price and define overage pricing.
- Visibility: detailed monthly usage breakdown (token counts, cache hit rates, model variants) to reconcile spend across product teams.
- Optimization levers: suggest quantization profiles, KV cache TTLs, and batching recommendations to lower unit cost — these can be included as professional services deliverables.

Legal redlines we typically see (and suggested counters):
- SLA credit caps: procurement pushes for unlimited credits; propose a reasonable cap (e.g., monthly credits limited to X% of monthly fee) tied to severity.
- Subcontracting: customers want to prevent subcontracting; include a clause allowing Redwood to use cloud providers and partners with notice and flow-down security obligations.
- Indemnity: limit Redwood indemnity to direct damages and cap at contract value; offer enhanced indemnity for specific regulatory needs as an add-on.

Sample procurement Q&A (for SAs/AEs to carry into meetings):
- Q: "How do you measure throughput?"
  A: We measure token throughput at the serving layer aggregated per pool per hour; metrics exported to your observability in near-real-time.
- Q: "Can we reserve burst capacity?"
  A: Yes — contracts can include a burst pool entitlement with defined consumption rate and replenishment rules.
- Q: "What models are covered under the SLA?"
  A: SLA defines model class buckets (small/medium/large). Specific model names and quantization states are enumerated in the SOW to set expectations.

Operationalized handoffs (post-signature):
- Week 0–2: onboarding plan — cluster provisioning, VPC peering, KMS setup, baseline soak test schedule.
- Week 3–6: POW/soak, telemetry baseline, finalize SLA thresholds based on empirical results.
- Ongoing: monthly capacity review, cost/throughput optimization sessions, quarterly architecture review.

Risk register (top risks and mitigations):
- Risk: Mismatch between customer's production workload and our baseline throughput assumptions.
  Mitigation: POW + explicit workload profile capture + conservative initial SLAs.
- Risk: Unexpected latency due to multi-tenancy leakage or noisy-neighbor effects.
  Mitigation: enforce isolation envelope, dedicated pools, and KV cache quotas.
- Risk: Procurement wants aggressive termination rights.
  Mitigation: offer transition assistance and phased pro-rata refunds tied to hardware procurement timelines.

Appendix: quick scripts/metrics to include in SOW (for eng/SRE teams)
- Definitions: token, request, model-class, sequence-length buckets, measurement window.
- Metrics to export: tokens/sec per pool, p50/p95/p99 latency, cache-hit ratio, GPU utilization, scheduled vs unscheduled downtime.
- Acceptance criteria for POW: defined p95 latency threshold and sustained tokens/sec for 48h with <Y% variance.

Notes to sales engineers:
- Avoid overpromising raw latency numbers without workload context (sequence length, model family, batch sizes matter).
- Use POW as leverage: it reduces procurement risk and gives both sides measurable acceptance criteria.
- Keep legal simple on subcontracting and data controls — escalate to Legal for unusual demands.

Next steps / action items:
- Convert this doc into a one-pager for procurement teams (owner: Marcus).
- Draft SOW template with variable placeholders for model-class, tokens/sec, and burst policy (owner: Elena).
- Prepare a standard POW checklist + telemetry dashboard template (owner: Ravi).

End of note.
